video_title: Bond Market Dominoes: The Path to 6% Rates
gist: Peter Boockvar argues the bond market, not the Kevin Warsh Fed, is setting the cost of capital as investors revolt against deficits (France as the problem child, US worse) and AI hyperscalers soak up ~$500B of debt, with long yields heading toward 6% and CCC spreads already above 1,000bp. He and Dan Nathan also cover AI agents eroding Big Tech moats (Meta's Muse vs Google), narrow two-lane market breadth, sticky oil supply losses, and deposit-cost pressure ahead of bank earnings.

insights.claim: The bond market entered 2026 pricing two Fed cuts but the Fed under Kevin Warsh is instead likely to deliver two hikes, after a unanimous hike despite Trump appointing Warsh expecting cuts.
insights.speaker: Peter Boockvar
insights.so_what: Policy path has flipped from easing to tightening; rate-cut-dependent trades are on the wrong side.
insights.quote: we entered the year uh the bond market was pricing in two cuts and instead we're probably going to get two hikes

insights.claim: The market is leading the Fed rather than the reverse: long-end yields are setting the cost of capital and dragged the Fed into its rate hike, making the Fed somewhat irrelevant.
insights.speaker: Peter Boockvar
insights.so_what: Watch the long end of the curve, not Fed guidance, for the true cost of capital.
insights.quote: I do think that the market is leading the Fed rather than the opposite and the Fed is really just following

insights.claim: Fed rate hikes are the wrong tool for current inflation, which stems from AI data center construction spending and crude supply shortfalls that higher policy rates cannot fix.
insights.speaker: Peter Boockvar
insights.so_what: Hikes may squeeze rate-sensitive sectors without curbing the supply-driven inflation sources.

insights.claim: Long-term US Treasury yields are just south of 5.5% and could head toward 6%, deepening crowding out as roughly $1 trillion of ~$5 trillion in federal revenue (20%) already goes to interest expense.
insights.speaker: Peter Boockvar
insights.so_what: A move to 6% would compound fiscal crowding out and pressure all duration assets.
insights.quote: the US government takes in about $5 trillion of revenue and about$1 trillion of that, so 20% of it is just going to interest expense

insights.claim: For the first time in decades bond investors are punishing excessive debts and deficits, first in Japan, then the US, and now acutely in Europe with France as the problem child.
insights.speaker: Peter Boockvar
insights.so_what: Fiscal profligacy is now priced; long-duration sovereign debt carries a new risk premium.

insights.claim: France's yield spike cannot be explained by growth (expected under 1%) and is primarily about years of excessive budget spending that politicians would not curb.
insights.speaker: Peter Boockvar
insights.so_what: French yields are a fiscal-credibility trade, not a growth trade.

insights.claim: French fiscal stress is spreading to Italian and possibly Spanish yields, while Germany outperforms as a flight-to-safety trade due to lower debt ratios.
insights.speaker: Peter Boockvar
insights.so_what: Expect periphery spread widening and Bund relative outperformance.

insights.claim: The US runs a larger budget deficit relative to GDP than France, so the French bond revolt is directly relevant to US Treasuries.
insights.speaker: Peter Boockvar
insights.so_what: US is not immune; the same fiscal repricing can hit Treasuries.
insights.quote: you know who's got a greater budget deficit relative to GDP than France uh we do uh here in the US

themes.theme: AI capex financing and credit contagion

insights.claim: Hyperscalers may issue up to $500 billion of debt this year, roughly double last year, competing with sovereigns for capital and pushing up yields.
insights.speaker: Peter Boockvar
insights.so_what: AI debt supply is a structural upward force on yields and credit spreads.
insights.quote: I've seen estimates up to $500 billion worth of debt this year

insights.claim: Free cash flow, the original funding source for AI capex, is exhausted, forcing companies into debt and even equity raises (e.g., Google), while Wall Street expects next year's capex to be 50% above 2026.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Rising capex plus external funding increases sensitivity to rates and investor appetite.

insights.claim: SpaceX plans to raise $40 billion including $30 billion of debt, and its CDS widened from about 130 to nearly 200bp, implying ~$200,000 per year to insure $10 million of bonds.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Credit markets are starting to charge more for AI/space mega-borrowers; neoclouds and Oracle trade wider still.

insights.claim: CCC high-yield spreads have broken above 1,000bp over Treasuries with CCC yields at 15%, and borrowers who locked ~3% loans in the euphoric 2021 market now face 8-9% on refinancing.
insights.speaker: Peter Boockvar
insights.so_what: Refinancing wall is already biting the weakest borrowers and real estate.
insights.quote: the triple C credit spread relative to treasuries has now broken above a thousand basis points. The yields in triple C is 15%

insights.claim: If OpenAI and Anthropic IPOs slip to late 2027 and public valuations fall, cross-holdings among Nvidia, Amazon, Google and others could make a private or public down round a contagion event.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Circular AI investments create domino risk if marks get cut.

insights.claim: AI capex is a bubble but the underlying technology is not; the debate is about what it costs to build it, not its value - 'a game of dominoes'.
insights.speaker: Peter Boockvar
insights.so_what: Separate the investable infrastructure cycle from the long-term technology payoff.
insights.quote: We're not debating here the quality of the technology and how it's going to change all our lives. We're debating what it takes to create that.

themes.theme: AI agents and Big Tech moat erosion

insights.claim: Meta's Muse agent launch sparked a roughly 40% rally from 52-week lows in weeks, offering monetization via transaction vig, subscriptions, consumption and its ~3 billion users, including un-monetized WhatsApp.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Upcoming Meta earnings and capex guidance must justify a faith-driven rally.

insights.claim: Agents may not be differentiated from one another, just as LLMs are hard to differentiate, so their profitability is uncertain even if they drive compute demand.
insights.speaker: Peter Boockvar
insights.so_what: Agent hype may boost compute names more than agent providers' margins.

insights.claim: Google's search business is at risk because users now rely on Gemini answers instead of clicking links, and Google underperformed Meta over the past month as Muse took the agent narrative.
insights.speaker: Peter Boockvar
insights.so_what: Search ad click economics face disruption; Google needs a consumer agent answer.
insights.quote: When was the last time, Dan, that you clicked when you went to Google and you clicked on one of the links?

insights.claim: Amazon has blocked personal agents from buying on its platform because agent purchases bypass ad clicks that fund its large advertising business.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Agentic commerce threatens retail-media ad revenue; expect walled gardens.

insights.claim: Mag 7 companies are now all in each other's businesses (cloud, agents, models), eroding the isolated moats that justified record multiples and raising the question of what multiple to pay.
insights.speaker: Peter Boockvar
insights.so_what: Competitive convergence argues for multiple compression across megacaps.

insights.claim: An FT Lex piece estimated AI agents could cost banks $500 billion by moving savers to better rates; Nathan's Instinct agent saved him $1,100 unprompted, suggesting consumers may pay for agents unlike search.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Agents threaten bank deposit franchises and may enable subscription monetization.

insights.claim: Only about 40% of NYSE stocks trade above their 200-day moving average versus 64% six weeks ago, reflecting a two-lane market where data centers lead and rate-, fuel- and inflation-sensitive retail and consumer names lag.
insights.speaker: Peter Boockvar
insights.so_what: Narrow breadth signals an unhealthy market per Bob Farrell's rule.
insights.quote: I think about 40% of the New York Stock Exchange stocks are trading above its 200 day moving average. About six weeks ago it was 64%.

insights.claim: Despite a nominal ceasefire, Iran struck a Saudi airport and Houthis hit a tanker near Qatar, with Brent at $105 and WTI at $93, and no Iran peace deal is expected soon.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Geopolitical premium in crude is sticky.

insights.claim: Crude flows through the Gulf are near pre-war levels but refined product flows remain a fraction of pre-war, and cumulative losses of billions of barrels keep prices elevated.
insights.speaker: Peter Boockvar
insights.so_what: Product (diesel/gasoline) tightness sustains inflation beyond crude headlines.

insights.claim: Saudi Aramco's CEO said normalizing inventories could take up to two years even if the war ended, because commercial stocks used to plug gaps are running out.
insights.speaker: Peter Boockvar
insights.so_what: Oil price downside is limited; any prolongation exposes depleted buffers.
insights.quote: we've sort of run out of band-aids

insights.claim: Banks sold off post-FOMC because the hike implies rising deposit costs as banks compete with higher-yielding money market funds, reversing expected relief from cuts.
insights.speaker: Peter Boockvar
insights.so_what: Net interest margin pressure is the key risk in Q3 bank prints.

insights.claim: Bank CEOs' 'resilient consumer' claims are largely nominal: 3-5% card spending growth with 3-4% inflation, much on gasoline, is not real strength.
insights.speaker: Peter Boockvar
insights.so_what: Deflate consumer spending data before reading it as strength.
